# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–22 (Complete – Updated 155)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer of sixth year** (Chapter 22 opening). Spring of sixth year (Chapter 21) completed with Rebecca's Court presentation triumph and Amelia's final maternal decision. Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, and elder Sir Pitt's death.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opens "It was the summer of the sixth year." Amelia's separation from George occurs in this summer. George's room (unopened for 10+ years) prepared; contains George's 1814 Army list, dictionary, Bible from his mother, spurs, dried inkstand, writing-book with his handwriting.
- **Locations**: Salwick; Harrowgate; Dunholt; London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Piccadilly, St. James's Street); Queen's Crawley; Court palace; Gaunt House; Gulton; Bryngate (market town; Fedette Orlwood, Madrek Orlwood, Colan, Maric Lindson, Cotho, Feena Stenworth residents); Lombard Street (bank); Calcutta (Jos); Madras (Major); Russell Square (Osborne residence); parsonage with lavender behind it.
- **Seasonal/environmental details**: Spring—wind off water with salt and tar smell; bees hum in lavender; vespers bell; frost silvered hedges earlier in season. Summer—river up in spring; rain threatening since morning but holding off; dog barking and going quiet.

## Main Characters

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)**
- **Court presentation achievement (Chapter 21)**: Gained presentation at Court through Lady Jane's sponsorship, pronounced "charmante." Used lace and brocade materials "quietly carried home."
- **Court jewels scheme (Chapter 21)**: Court diamonds hired from Mr. Polonius of Coventry Street; **never returned**. Pitt gave diamond clasp; blushed when mentioned. Steyne financed diamonds, hidden in Amelia's old desk containing valuables unknown to Rawdon.
- **Post-presentation virtue performance**: Cuts dubious acquaintances; instructs Smith to deny callers; performs intense loyalty to King; commissioned royal portrait from Colnaghi's; wears portrait in brooch. Narrator notes some rouge won't come off; some so good tears won't disturb it.
- **Gaunt House musical triumph (Chapter 21)**: Sang very best; men crowded round piano; women enemies left alone; Paul Jefferson Jones praised her singing, claiming conquest of Lady Gaunt through it.
- **Financial transactions (Chapter 21)**: Bank arrangement (Messrs. Jones, Brown, and Robinson, Lombard Street) providing substantial sum; distributed money to Briggs, Raggles, and livery-man Spavin strategically.
- **Maternal rejection (unchanged)**: Would have preferred to leave little Rawdon behind.

**Sir Pitt Crawley (younger) – Baronet, MP**
- **Parliamentary ambition and dissembling**: Profound dissembler; attends assiduously; learns House routine thoroughly; makes acquaintance with ministers and party chiefs.
- **Emotional dependency on Rebecca intensifying**: Returns daily with increasing gladness; felt pang at departing for Christmas.
- **Court presentation duty**: Drove to Curzon Street in glittering uniform with sword to convey Rebecca; acted as escort after presentation.
- **Secret gift to Rebecca**: Gave diamond clasp confined to pearl necklace; omitted mentioning to Lady Jane; blushed when mentioned.
- **Financial circumstances**: Knows brother's family has nothing; gave draft on bankers for hundred pounds before Christmas.

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley**
- **Complete subjugation**: "Beat and cowed into laziness and submission." Bold reckless blood turned into torpid, submissive, middle-aged, stout gentleman.
- **Deceived regarding jewels**: Knew nothing about brilliant diamonds; believed Rebecca hired them; Steyne knew truth.
- **Unaware of Steyne arrangement**: Heard Becky laughing at night; unaware of her financial transactions and manipulations.
- **Strong attachment to little Rawdon**: Wraps boy in shawls; hoists onto coach roof; walks and rides with brother Pitt.

**Little Rawdon (Son)**
- **Character and activities**: Fine open-faced boy with blue eyes and waving flaxen hair; about eight years old; generous and soft in heart. Image of his father. Coming from school on May half-holiday, flushed with health, singing, bundle of school-books by thong.

**Amelia Osborne (Mrs. George Osborne)**
- **Final maternal decision and letter (Chapter 21 – UPDATED)**: Wrote letter to Miss Osborne (Russell Square) explaining reasons for giving up boy. Father's fresh misfortunes ruined him; her pittance barely supports parents, insufficient for George's advantages. Despite great suffering at parting, willing by God's help to endure for boy's sake. Knows those receiving him will make him happy. Described George's disposition—quick, impatient of control, easily moved by love and kindness. **Stipulation**: Demanded written agreement to see child as often as wished; could not part under other terms. Letter made Miss Osborne blush; look toward her glooming father.
- **Giving up the boy (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: 
  - **Before separation**: Days passed in parleys, visits, preparations. Widow broke matter to Georgy with great caution; expected him much affected; he was rather **elated than otherwise**, bragging to boys at school about living with grandfather, becoming rich, getting carriage, pony, finer school, buying Leader's pencil-case and paying tart-woman.
  - **On departure day (summer of sixth year)**: Carriage drove up; George in new suit (tailor measured him previously); boy sprung up with sun putting on new clothes; mother heard him from room where she had been lying in speechless grief and watching.
  - **Preparations made**: Days before, made preparations purchasing stores, marking books and linen, talking with him and preparing him for change—fondly fancying he needed preparation. Tears fell into boxes; passages scored in favorite books; old toys, relics, treasures hoarded and packed with strange care—**boy took no note**. Made thousand eager declarations about what he'd do with grandfather; showed how little parting cast him down. Said he would come see mama often on pony, fetch her in carriage, drive in park, she should have everything wanted.
  - **Maternal anguish**: Mother fain to content herself with his selfish demonstrations, convinced herself son loved her. Owns that her own selfishness and imprudent love denied him his just rights and pleasures. Narrator comments: "I know few things more affecting than that timorous debasement and self-humiliation of a woman." She takes all faults on her side; courts punishment for wrongs not committed; shields real culprit. "It is those who injure women who get the most kindness from them."
  - **Father's confession (Chapter 21)**: Old gentleman revealed entire truth—his son (Jos) **still paying the annuity** despite appearance of abandonment. Old Sedley's imprudence had flung it away; concealed truth extended period. Confessed with trembling, miserable voice. Amelia fell on his neck kissing him many times, crying "You are always good and kind. It is not for the money...my God! my God! have mercy upon me, and give me strength to bear this trial." Father didn't know her tears meant she was conquered.
- **Letter to Jos (Chapter 21)**: Wrote tender supplication to brother at Calcutta imploring him not to withdraw support granted to parents, painting condition in artless pathos. Did not know truth—Jos's annuity still regular but money-lender in City receiving it; old Sedley sold it for sum to prosecute bootless schemes. Calculated eagerly time before answer arrived; wrote down date in pocket-book.
- **Regarding Major at Madras**: Had not communicated griefs to him; not written since congratulating on approaching marriage. Thought with sickening despondency that only friend who felt such regard was fallen away.
- **Physical and emotional decline**: Grows daily more care-worn and sad, fixing alarmed eyes on child unable to interpret expression. Starts up at night, peeps into his room stealthily. Sleeps little. Weeps and prays in long silent nights. Before separation, passed many long solitary hours in making preparations, silent misery.
- **Old desk (unchanged)**: Years ago gave Rebecca a desk now containing Rebecca's diamonds and valuables hidden from Rawdon.

**Old Mr. Sedley**
- **Financial decline and deception (Chapter 21)**: Dabbled in speculation despite Clapp's remonstrances; wine and coal companies failed; bills in arrear. **Sold Jos's annuity**: Received sum to prosecute bootless schemes; concealed from family extended period. Confessed with trembling, miserable voice.
- **Receives hundred pounds (Chapter 22)**: Amelia kissed him, placed bill for hundred pounds in his hands. Said "don't be harsh with Georgy. He—he is not going to stop with us long."

**Miss Osborne (Old Osborne's daughter)**
- **Receives Amelia's letter (Chapter 21 – UPDATED)**: Letter made her blush; looked toward her glooming father. Next day visited Amelia according to promise in note. Meeting between them **friendly**.
- **Evaluation of Amelia (Chapter 21 – UPDATED)**: Cold, sensible, not unkind. Poor widow realized no fear lest Miss Osborne take first place in son's affection. Had Osborne been better looking, younger, more affectionate, warmer-hearted, mother might not have been so pleased. Miss Osborne thought of old times and memories; touched by poor mother's pitiful situation. **Conquered, laying down arms, humbly submitted**. That day arranged preliminaries of capitulation treaty.
- **Prepares George's room (Chapter 21 – UPDATED)**: Room unopened for 10+ years; contained George's clothes, papers, handkerchiefs, whips, caps, fishing-rods, sporting gear. 1814 Army list with name on cover; little dictionary; Bible mother gave him on mantelpiece with pair of spurs and dried inkstand covered with dust of ten years. Room symbol of frozen grief. Miss Osborne much affected entering with servants; sank quite pale on little bed. Housekeeper said: "This is blessed news, m'am...good old times returning...dear little feller...but some folks in May Fair, m'am, will owe him grudge, m'am." Housekeeper clicked back bolt holding window-sash letting air into chamber.

**Old Mr. Osborne**
- **Reaction to Amelia's letter (Chapter 22 – NEW)**: When Miss Osborne read letter with tremulous eager voice, said "What? Mrs. Pride has come down, has she? Reg'lar starved out, hey? Ha, ha! I knew she would." Tried keeping dignity and reading paper; could not follow it. Chuckled and swore behind sheet. Commanded: "Get the room over mine--his room that was--ready." Could not suppress satisfaction.

**The Marquis of Steyne**
- **Financing Rebecca's scheme (Chapter 21)**: Present at Court; financed Rebecca's court diamonds. Made bank arrangement providing substantial sum. Observed Rebecca sing Mozart at Gaunt House, moving Lady Steyne to tears. Declared himself master of Gaunt House; forces family obedience through bullying and threats.

**Lady Steyne**
- **Musical responsiveness (Chapter 21)**: Held "very highest rank in Vanity Fair"; severe, spotless, beautiful. Convent childhood with beloved organist sister; religious devotion preserved. Moved to tears by Rebecca's Mozart singing.

**Minor Characters - Bryngate/Regional Residents**
- **Colan**: Remarked river up again (Chapter 22).
- **Fedette Orlwood**: Said river always up in spring (Chapter 22).
- **Madrek Orlwood**: Never kept promise made to Ilena Orlwood to rebuild fallen wall at Fenmere; matter abandoned (Chapter 22).
- **Maric Lindson**: Found work in Bryngate; talked of weather, harvest, lame horse with Cotho (Chapter 22).
- **Cotho**: Discussed weather, harvest, lame horse with Maric; remarked "price of salt is scandal" (Chapter 22).
- **Feena Stenworth**: Agreed "scandal" regarding salt price (Chapter 22).
- **Isbin and Zanar Hollwood**: Mentioned as window-mending characters (Chapters 21–22); possibly mending torn sleeves by window (variant readings suggest possible textual confusion).
- **Nelde Corrett**: Fell asleep in chair before fire caught (Chapter 22).
- **Rorine**: Mended torn sleeve by window, said little (Chapter 22).
- **Movie**: Laughed at story nobody else found funny (Chapter 22).

## Critical Facts (Chapters 21–22 – UPDATED)
- **Amelia's absolute surrender (Chapter 22)**: **The separation is happening now, summer of sixth year**. George departs to live with Old Osborne. Child completely unaffected by separation; elated and eager. Mother's heart breaking while child goes smiling away. Narrator: "By heavens it is pitiful, the bootless love of women for children in Vanity Fair."
- **Miss Osborne's capitulation**: Conquered by Amelia's pitiful situation; humbly submitted; arranged treaty preliminaries.
- **Old Osborne's satisfaction**: Barely suppressed delight; knew Mrs. "Pride" starved out; commanded room prepared; could not follow paper with satisfaction.
- **Steyne's control over Rebecca**: Finances her; knows diamond truth; provides bank access; maintains her dependency.
- **Jos's annuity continues**: Still paying despite Old Sedley's deception; money-lender in City receiving payments; Sedley sold annuity for capital to pursue schemes.
